title: DAY ONE
subtitle: THE HIGHWAY · PART 1
voice_hint: deep calm male narrator, documentary tone

scenes.narration: Day one of the outbreak. The highway is a trap.
Sam grabs his keys and heads for the highway.
scenes.caption: BIG MISTAKE

scenes.narration: So does everyone else. Nothing moves.
scenes.caption: GRIDLOCK

scenes.narration: In 2005, millions fled Houston before Hurricane Rita. The jam stretched over 160 kilometres.
scenes.caption: 160 KM JAM

scenes.narration: Cars ran dry in the heat. Dozens died on the road, before the storm arrived.
scenes.caption: BEFORE THE STORM

scenes.narration: Sam leaves the car. Behind him, the horns fall silent.
Then something starts moving between the lanes.
He grabs a bike from a pickup. Eighteen kilometres an hour beats gridlock.
scenes.caption: 18 KM/H

scenes.narration: By sunset, he finds a farm. The taps are empty.
Sam knows a trick. The basement water heater holds 150 litres of drinkable water.
scenes.caption: 150 LITRES

scenes.narration: On day two, something scratches at the door. Just a dog.
Would you have stayed in the car? Follow for part two.

sources.claim: Rita jam on I-45 north of Houston ran more than 100 miles (160+ km) and had lasted about a day and a half; ~100 F heat; stranded cars
Rita evacuee travel times were 18-24 hours (vs 6-8 for Ike); one evacuee's normally sub-4-hour drive to Dallas took 25 hours
~3.7 million left the Houston region; dozens died on the road (bus fire, crashes, heat stroke); Houston was only grazed
Service stations ran out of fuel during the Rita evacuation; police carried gasoline to stranded drivers
Nursing-home evacuee bus fire near Dallas killed 23 (NTSB figure; early reports said 24)
Houston Chronicle retrospective: Rita's mass evacuation left about 100 people dead
US residential tanks are typically 40-50 gal (about 151-189 L), up to 75-80 gal for large households
European household boilers are typically 30-150 L (CE Delft sizing table)
FEMA: the hot water heater is an emergency water source - turn off power, let it cool, open the drain valve at the bottom
Dutch national cycling count: city averages 14.4 km/h (Amsterdam) to 16.9 km/h (Arnhem)
Measured path speeds of cyclists vary between 15 and 25 km/h
Strava-based average for road riders on mostly flat terrain is about 24 km/h (so 25 is the top of the range, not typical)
